title: Japanese Fir: Ancient Japanese Firs You Can Visit
meta_description: Momi, the Japanese fir of cool upland shrine groves. Around Higashi-Hiroshima several stand past three metres round, measured but never dated.
intro: Momi, the Japanese fir, is a warm-temperate species of Honshu and Kyushu that favours cool upland shrine groves and dislikes heat. The old ones here grow within a few kilometres of each other in the hills around Higashi-Hiroshima, and none carries a recorded age: Japan's giant-tree register measures girth, not years. Uneyama Shrine's fir, at 3.4 metres, stands in a grove the prefecture designated in 1987 and later lost trees to a typhoon; written accounts of the grove name five other species and never this one. Hongu Hachiman's, also 3.4 metres, shares its hilltop with cedars by the dozen and a 1701 hall the city protects as an important cultural property. Ashuku Hachiman's matches them, and the one behind Morimasa Shrine measured exactly three metres in the 2000 survey, which is to say it qualified for the register by nothing at all.
